documents.excerpt: When God confronts, corrects, disciplines, or crushes a person, in which direction does the spirit break?
excerpts: When God confronts, corrects, disciplines, or crushes a person, in which direction does the spirit break?

A wrong spirit breaks away into defensiveness, blame, bitterness, anger, performance, hiding, or despair; a right spirit breaks toward God in confession, humility, dependence, surrender, praise, and hope.
A right spirit is not one that never breaks—everyone’s spirit will break—but one that breaks in the right direction.

Merciful destruction
David had asked that the bones God crushed rejoice. God broke the wrong spirit so he could build the right one.

God did not destroy David; he destroyed the pride threatening to destroy David. Sometimes God breaks in order to rebuild.

August 10, 2026
Renew Me
A bent heart needs new birth, not a tune-up
Hearts drift naturally away from God; people accidentally become worldly, not holy, disciplined in prayer, or Christlike. Elijah echoes J. C. Ryle’s image of a stone naturally moving downward.
Better habits and surroundings cannot supply the needed new heart. Ezekiel promised a heart of flesh in place of stone, and Jesus demanded new birth—not improvement, reform, or polish.
Because dead people cannot raise themselves, Christianity is not behavior modification but God’s act of making the spiritually dead alive and new by the Holy Spirit.
If the deepest problem is nature rather than merely record, only the God who formed the heart can create the clean heart David seeks.

excerpts: Josh thanks the Father for Scripture, Hebrews, and the supremacy of Jesus from beginning to end.
He thanks Jesus for "humbling yourself, taking our flesh," living the life sinners could not live, dying the death they deserved, and taking their place.
Addressing the crucified King, he prays, "All things were made through you and for you," yet the creation mocked its maker.

Josh recalls the mockery, "You can save others. Why can’t you save yourself?" and says Jesus stayed on the cross because he saw "this joy"—a redeemed family of faith called to trust, serve, love, and change the world.

He asks the Lord for needed power, help to forgive others and themselves, and grace to walk faithfully; he closes by thanking God for the series, Jesus, and the cross, then prays in Jesus’ name, "Amen."

documents.excerpt: Josh defines punishment as justice rendered. God does not overlook sin, but for those in Christ the required justice fell on Jesus rather than on them.
excerpts: Josh defines punishment as justice rendered. God does not overlook sin, but for those in Christ the required justice fell on Jesus rather than on them.

He layers apostolic and prophetic claims: people dead in sin are made alive with Christ; Jesus bore sins and drank the cup of God’s wrath to the last drop so believers could receive blessing; Isaiah says the punishment bringing peace fell on him; Paul says there is now no condemnation; and believers have peace with God through Christ.
Hardship is therefore not God getting even. Jesus paid it all. God may be bringing a wandering child back, but he is not making Christ’s finished payment again.

Believers instead come to Mount Zion, the living God’s heavenly city, joyful angels, the church of the firstborn, God the Judge, perfected righteous spirits, Jesus the new-covenant mediator, and sprinkled blood speaking better than Abel’s.
The passage warns against refusing the heavenly speaker, promises another shaking that removes created things, and commands thankful, reverent worship because the received kingdom cannot be shaken and God is a consuming fire.
documents.title: Hebrews contrasts two mountains and warns hearers not to refuse God — Keep Running!

Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, whose faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, shut lions’ mouths, quenched flames, and turned weakness into strength.
Gideon was a fearful farmer, Barak faced an overwhelming army, and Samson accomplished great feats despite deep flaws.
Their stories emphasize not human greatness but God’s faithfulness to work through trusting people—even when they are a mess.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 29, 2026 · By Faith
documents.excerpt: Josh recalls attending a Jessica Simpson concert as a high-school freshman, entering an onstage singing contest despite not knowing her songs, winning the crowd’s approval, and receiving unusual backstage access.
excerpts: Josh recalls attending a Jessica Simpson concert as a high-school freshman, entering an onstage singing contest despite not knowing her songs, winning the crowd’s approval, and receiving unusual backstage access.
After the other contestants leave, he meets Simpson’s family and is seated onstage, where she kisses and serenades him; he later jokes that she was a shadow of a better woman, Kristen.
The experience briefly transformed his social confidence, but the imposing security guard’s warning made clear that no one entered the protected area without authorization.
Josh uses the comic story to introduce the far more serious confidence Hebrews gives ordinary believers to enter God’s presence.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 29, 2026 · By Faith
documents.excerpt: Believers enter a place they could never claim for themselves because Jesus has unlocked it. Unlike an old covenant high priest who entered alone, Christ leaves the way open and is himself the door through whom people come to God.
excerpts: Believers enter a place they could never claim for themselves because Jesus has unlocked it. Unlike an old covenant high priest who entered alone, Christ leaves the way open and is himself the door through whom people come to God.

Josh asks the church to remember the sentence, “Jesus unlocked the new and living way.” It is new because the old covenant is obsolete in its light, and living because Christ has an indestructible life and always lives to intercede.
When Christ’s flesh was torn and his life sacrificed, God tore the temple curtain. That event signified open access for all who believe.
Believers may therefore enter boldly rather than fearfully; Josh joins this confidence to the assurance that perfect love drives out fear and identifies Jesus as perfect love.

2026-06-29
June 29, 2026
By Faith
Jesus enters, leaves the door open, and becomes the door
Believers enter a place they could never claim for themselves because Jesus has unlocked it. Unlike an old covenant high priest who entered alone, Christ leaves the way open and is himself the door through whom people come to God.
Josh asks the church to remember the sentence, “Jesus unlocked the new and living way.” It is new because the old covenant is obsolete in its light, and living because Christ has an indestructible life and always lives to intercede.
When Christ’s flesh was torn and his life sacrificed, God tore the temple curtain. That event signified open access for all who believe.
Believers may therefore enter boldly rather than fearfully; Josh joins this confidence to the assurance that perfect love drives out fear and identifies Jesus as perfect love.

Isaiah’s Creator-Creation Distinction
After greeting the church on Father’s Day, Josh quotes Isaiah to establish that God’s thoughts and ways transcend humanity’s as the heavens transcend the earth.
The wonder is not that human language can contain God completely, but that the all-knowing, all-powerful, ever-present God chooses to make himself understandable through it.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · June 22, 2026 · By Faith
documents.excerpt: Josh explores apparently risky biblical comparisons: Jesus’ arrival carries a thief’s surprise without a thief’s character, while shepherd, slave, father, king, and husband imagery each illuminates one aspect of God and leaves others in shadow.
excerpts: Josh explores apparently risky biblical comparisons: Jesus’ arrival carries a thief’s surprise without a thief’s character, while shepherd, slave, father, king, and husband imagery each illuminates one aspect of God and leaves others in shadow.
He playfully extends the thief image through a song in which the enemy thought he had the believer, but Jesus answers, ‘You are mine.’
Because no human word, picture, or experience fits God perfectly, hearers must ask what part of each comparison is intended and what part is not.
God’s condescension in using human language reflects the love that brought him down to humanity’s level.

Every Analogy Is a Spotlight, Not a Complete Portrait
Josh explores apparently risky biblical comparisons: Jesus’ arrival carries a thief’s surprise without a thief’s character, while shepherd, slave, father, king, and husband imagery each illuminates one aspect of God and leaves others in shadow.

As the church comes to the table, Josh prays that humility will displace pride and concern for others’ opinions, that people will draw near through Christ, tie onto the anchor, and hold on.

documents.excerpt: Steve reads Hebrews 5:3 and 8–10. Traditional priests needed sacrifices for their own sins as well as the people’s, while the Son learned obedience through suffering, became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey, and was designated high priest in Melchizedek’s order.
excerpts: Steve reads Hebrews 5:3 and 8–10. Traditional priests needed sacrifices for their own sins as well as the people’s, while the Son learned obedience through suffering, became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey, and was designated high priest in Melchizedek’s order.
Sinful priests could offer only temporary help. Repeated animal sacrifices covered sin without finishing the work; Jesus did not merely bring a sacrifice but became the sacrifice and washed sin away.

Steve clarifies that being ‘made perfect’ does not imply that Jesus was formerly sinful. His already-perfect obedience was completed in action and suffering at the cross. Children’s promises to do chores illustrate the difference between verbal agreement and costly follow-through, down to taking out trash that spills coffee grounds and cleaning up after the dog.
Christ’s death and resurrection completed the work. His once-for-all, everlasting priesthood means mercy and grace do not expire and sacrifice need not be repeated.

Steve quotes Jesus’ final cry, ‘It is finished,’ then Hebrews 10:12: after offering one sacrifice for sins for all time, Jesus sat at God’s right hand. Standing Levitical priests could not rest because their work continued; Jesus’ seated posture declares payment complete.

excerpts: The warning can benefit skeptics, but Josh says it is directed to believers: a great truth has been heard, yet without the most careful attention surrounding currents can carry it away.
First-century Jewish Christians deeply honored the Old Testament, but even they were warned about dismissing God’s greatest word to humanity, the good news of Christ.

Peter’s picture of the devil prowling like a lion reveals an enemy intent on stealing the precious gospel possession. Josh warns that baptism and public profession do not end the attack; Satan celebrates when a public Christian lives a weak faith.

The Holy Spirit equips believers to fight the good fight and guides them into truth. Anticipating Hebrews 6, Josh says God’s promises are a secure anchor: when drift occurs, the anchor has not moved; the believer has allowed slack through irresponsibility, laziness, or neglect.

excerpts: Returning to Hebrews 2:2–3a, Josh says “violation” or “transgression” concerns sins of commission, while “disobedience” suggests sins of omission. Sin includes both doing what God forbids and failing to do what God commands.
Avoiding robbery does not fulfill the command to love one’s neighbor, and refusing to curse an enemy is not the same as praying for that enemy. Omission can therefore be as troubling as commission.

A rapid church quiz illustrates the categories: David’s adultery with Bathsheba is commission; Jonah’s flight from Nineveh is active commission rooted in resistance to mercy; Adam’s passivity while Eve is deceived is omission; and Moses striking the rock instead of speaking to it is commission.

Grace does not eliminate the Lord’s discipline. Jesus’ warning that much is required from those given much leads Josh to summarize: commission does what God hates, omission fails to do what God loves, and Hebrews 2 says both are judged. Neglect is especially dangerous because it can destroy while a person feels safe.

excerpts: Josh says that if believers do not even know their gifts, he is failing them.
Josh compares physical birth certificates with the absence of a “new life certificate” listing spiritual gifts. Discovery requires action, and most believers likely possess several gifts.

He urges hearers to take the church’s available gifts assessment and then ask an elder or pastor for help interpreting and deploying the result. He names prophecy, service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leadership, mercy, wisdom, discernment, faith, healing, miracles, tongues, helps, and administration.

The participation numbers trouble him: only two of ten who begin the assessment finish, and only half of those find a use in the body. Even allowing other ways to discover gifts, Josh says that if the assessment were the only route, only forty people in the church would be using their gifts; the pattern pictures widespread drift.

The modern church drifts not only when people skip Sunday but when they refuse daily church life and participation. Families that do not teach children to value the body deprive others of God’s gifts. The Spirit gives, Scripture governs, and the church is built; gifts serve and strengthen salvation rather than distracting from it.

documents.context: Josh Wyatt · May 11, 2026 · By Faith
documents.excerpt: Christian drift grows when people forget that Jesus is still helping. Because temptation never conquered him, he is both qualified and willing to help.
excerpts: Christian drift grows when people forget that Jesus is still helping. Because temptation never conquered him, he is both qualified and willing to help.
Josh explicitly opens the Amplified Bible and reads Hebrews 2:18: the one who suffered temptation, testing, and trial is able immediately to “run to the cry of” those exposed to the same suffering.
Angels can minister, but only Jesus runs to the cry and wipes tears. The high priest does not merely say “try harder”; he says to lean on and call on him.
Josh quotes Jesus’ words, “Neither do I condemn you. Go and sin no more,” and urges hearers not to hide when tempted but to run to Christ for grace.
If a believer sins, Jesus is also an advocate before God, and sincere confession receives forgiveness. Help is available both in resisting temptation and after failure.
